title: Ionisation energy
group: CHEM-ATOM / CHEM-PER — Atoms & the Periodic Table
examples: What makes the first ionisation energy change across a period?
Why are the second and third ionisation energies usually much higher?
Can you explain the effect of electron shells on ionisation energy?

explain.say: Today we say we are looking at ionisation energy changes. This energy is the energy needed to remove an electron from a neutral atom.
We say the first ionisation energy generally increases across a period. This is because the nuclear charge increases across the period.
We say there are dips in the trend when a stable electron configuration is reached. For example, going from Group 2 to Group 13 shows this dip.
We say the second and subsequent ionisation energies are always much higher. This is because you are removing an electron from a stable, inner shell.
For a real life example we say consider the noble gases like neon. They have a full outer shell. This makes them very stable atoms.
The most common mistake is saying that ionisation energy only depends on the number of protons. Remember that electron shielding also plays a very important role.

faq.q: Why is the first ionisation energy lower going from Group 2 to Group 13?
faq.a: This is because Group 13 elements have one electron in a p orbital. Removing this electron is easier than removing the two electrons from the full s and p orbitals of Group 2.
asks: Why does the trend dip there?
What causes the dip in IE values?

faq.q: Why does the energy jump so much after removing the first electron?
faq.a: The jump is large because you are now removing an electron from a completely filled, stable inner shell. These inner electrons are held very tightly by the nucleus.
asks: Why is IE2 so much bigger than IE1?
What happens when you remove a core electron?

faq.q: Does the size of the atom affect the ionisation energy?
faq.a: Yes, generally larger atoms have lower first ionisation energies. This is because the outermost electrons are further from the nucleus and are shielded more effectively.
asks: How does atomic size relate to IE?
Is there a link between atomic radius and IE?

faq.q: What is the difference between ionisation energy and electron affinity?
faq.a: Ionisation energy is the energy you must put in to take an electron away. Electron affinity is the energy released when an atom gains an electron.
asks: Are these two energy measurements related?
What is the difference between gaining and losing electrons?

faq.q: Does the trend always increase across a period?
faq.a: No, the trend increases but it can dip at certain groups, like the dip between Group 2 and Group 13, due to orbital stability.
asks: Are there exceptions to the increasing trend?
When is the trend not strictly increasing?

facts: Ionisation energy is the energy required to remove the most loosely held electron.
Across a period, IE generally increases due to increasing nuclear charge.
A large jump in successive IE indicates the removal of a core electron.
The stability of electron configurations influences the measured ionisation energy.

wrong.0: This ignores the crucial role of electron shielding in determining the energy.

wrong.1: While noble gases are stable, the jump is specifically about the second electron removal.

quiz.say: Which of the following elements would show the largest relative increase between its first and second ionisation energy?
quiz.why: Group 2 elements have a full s and p subshell configuration, making the removal of the second electron much more difficult.

wrong.1: These elements are stable with their outer shell, but the jump magnitude is typically smaller than for Group 2.
wrong.2: The first electron is relatively easy to remove, and the second is from a core shell, but the jump is not as pronounced as in Group 2.
wrong.3: While stable, the jump is best exemplified by the transition from a filled valence shell to a filled core shell.
